item.title: Project Euler - 15 - Lattice paths
item.description:
In this post we are dealing with Project Euler - 15 - Lattice paths. This is one of the simple dynamic programming problems. We have to find the number of paths to reach the bottom right from the top left, moving only downwards and right sidewards. It was not so easy for me to see the solution even for the sample data given. It would be easy when we look from the bottom-left. For the sample 2x2 grid, lets say the bottom-left (2, 2) point has 0 path and 1,2 and 2,1 have 1 path each. It is evident that number of paths to reach (2, 2) from all the points on the bottom most row (0, 2), (1, 2) and the right most column (2, 0), (2, 1), as we cannot move upwards and left sidewards. Now, (1, 1) has two paths to reach (2, 2), either through (1, 2) or (2, 1). So it has the value 2. Same way, (0, 1) and (1, 0) have 3 ways ( (0, 1) can take (1, 1) (which has 2 paths to (2, 2) ) and (0, 2) (which has 1 path to (2, 2) ). So, (0, 0) has 6 paths to (2, 2) either via (0, 1) or via (1, 0). Applied this idea as a dynamic programming program and it solved this problem.\\

 1Total = 21
 2
 3Array = [[0]*Total for i in xrange(Total)]
 4for i in xrange(Total): Array[i][Total - 1], Array[Total - 1][i] = 1, 1   #Initializing bottom row and right column with 1
 5
 6def Rec(i, j):
 7    global Array
 8    if Array[i][j]: return Array[i][j]
 9    Rec(i+1, j)
10    Rec(i, j+1)
11    Array[i][j] = Array[i+1][j] + Array[i][j+1]
12
13Rec (0, 0)
14print Array[0][0]

item.title: Project Euler - 14 - Longest Collatz sequence - memoization
item.description:
This post is about the Project Euler - 14 - Longest Collatz sequence problem. This is one of the perfect examples of memoization technique. This is the actual problem.
\\

The following iterative sequence is defined for the set of positive integers:

n → n/2 (n is even)
n → 3n + 1 (n is odd)

Using the rule above and starting with 13, we generate the following sequence:
13 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1

It can be seen that this sequence (starting at 13 and finishing at 1) contains 10 terms. Although it has not been proved yet (Collatz Problem), it is thought that all starting numbers finish at 1.

Which starting number, under one million, produces the longest chain?

NOTE: Once the chain starts the terms are allowed to go above one million.

\\

Simple Solution

\\ The problem statement looks pretty simple and a brute force will work just fine. This code runs in 20 seconds.
\\

 1def Series(N):
 2    Counter = 1
 3    while N != 1:
 4        N = N/2 if N % 2 == 0 else 3*N+1
 5        Counter += 1
 6    return Counter
 7
 8Max, Element = 0, 0
 9for x in xrange (1, 1000000):
10    series = Series(x)
11    if (Max < series):
12        Max = series
13        Element = x
14
15print Max, Element

\\ \\ As I had to wait for 20 seconds to get the solution, I was thinking about improving the performance. Then I found this. From the problem statement, 13 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1, starting with any number, if it becomes 13 at any point of time, it has to take the same route and if it becomes 13 it will take 10 steps to become 1. So I wanted to store this information first time itself, so that I don't have to recalculate. This is called Memoization. Quoting from wikipedia
\\

In computing, memoization is an optimization technique used primarily to speed up computer programs by having function calls avoid repeating the calculation of results for previously processed inputs

\\

Optimized (Memoized) Solution

\\ To optimize it, I just had to change the Series function alone. I stored the computed values in a dictionary and if the current number in the sequence happens to be in the dictionary, I ll just return the value corresponding to it. This program responded with the result in 2 seconds. That is 10 times faster than the first version.
\\

 1Dict = {}
 2
 3def Series(N):
 4    Counter = 1   #It is 1, because we are counting the initial N
 5    Original = N
 6    while N != 1:
 7        N = N/2 if N % 2 == 0 else 3*N+1
 8        if N in Dict:                    # Check if the length has been computed for this number already
 9            Counter += Dict[N]           # Add it to the current length counter
10            Dict [Original] = Counter    # Store the computed value for future look back
11            return Counter
12        Counter += 1
13    Dict [Original] = Counter            # Store the computed value for future look back
14    return Counter

\\ \\ \\ \\

item.title: Project Euler - Problem 18, Problem 67 - Maximum path sum
item.description:
Its been quite sometime since I did some coding. Last Sunday, one of the best friends of mine (Clement Lloyd) asked me if I can solve Project Euler's Problem 18. The problem name is Maximum path sum. Finally I got some time today and it is a simple Dynamic Programming Problem. The basic idea is to, keep on adding two adjacent elements of each row with the corresponding element in the previous row and keep the maximum of them. For example,
\\

 8
1 2

\\ The maximum of 8+1 and 8+2 would be 10 and 10 would take 8's place. So we keep on doing this till we reach the top. For the sample input
\\

3
  7 4
 2 4 6
8 5 9 3

\\ After first Iteration,
\\

3
   7  4
 10 13 15

\\ After second Iteration,
\\

3
  20 19

\\ After third Iteration,
\\

23

\\ Here is the solution which I used
\\

 1import sys
 2sys.stdin  = open ("Input.txt")
 3sys.stdout = open ("Output.txt", "w")
 4Array = []
 5for line in sys.stdin: Array.append (map (int, line.split()))
 6Array.reverse()
 7temp_array = [0] * (len(Array) + 1)
 8for Row in Array:
 9 for i in xrange (len(Row)):
10  temp_array[i] = Row[i] + max (temp_array[i], temp_array[i + 1])
11print max (temp_array)

\\ This solution will solve Project Euler's Problem 67 as well.
\\ \\ \\

item.title: SPOJ - ACODE - AlphaCode
item.description:
Problem Description - http://www.spoj.com/problems/ACODE/
\\ Approach :
\\

  1. Initialize an Array of Size N with 0 and element 0 as 1\\
  2. Loop through all the elements\\
  3. If it is a valid single digit number, Copy the previous element's value to the current element (DP[i] = DP[i-1])\\
  4. If it is a valid two digit number, Add the previous to previous element's value to the current element (DP[i] += DP[i-2])\\

\\ In one line : DP[i] = DP[i-1] {if valid single digit number} + DP[i-2] {if current and previous elements make a valid two digit number}
\\ Solution:\\

 1# include <cstdio>
 2# include <cstring>
 3char Input[5001] = "";
 4unsigned long long DP[5001];
 5int main()
 6{
 7 freopen ("Input.txt", "r", stdin);
 8 freopen ("Scratch.txt", "w", stdout);
 9 scanf ("%s", Input);
10 while (strcmp(Input, "0"))
11 {
12  int Len = strlen (Input), Index = 1;
13  memset (DP, 0, sizeof DP);
14  DP[0] = 1;
15  while (Index  9) DP[Index] += DP[Index-2 < 0?0:Index-2];
16   //printf ("%d\t%llu\n",Index, DP[Index]);
17   Index++;
18  }
19  //printf ("%llu\t%s\n", DP[Len-1], Input);
20  printf ("%llu\n", DP[Len-1]);
21  scanf ("%s", Input);
22 }
23}

item.title: Timus - 1018 - Binary Apple Tree - Dynamic Programming
item.description:
Today, I saw this interesting problem.
\\ Timus - 1018 - Binary Apple Tree
\\ When I started working on this, I didnt know why do we need Dynamic Programming to solve this. My idea was pretty simple.

  1. While reading Inputs find the total number of apples\\
  2. Find all the leaf Branches (I mean branches without any branches on them)\\
  3. Get the branch with the least number of apples and remove that\\
  4. Goto Step 2 until N - Q - 1 times. (N is the total number of enumerated points on the tree, Q is the number of branches to keep, Always there will be N - 1 branches on the binary tree. So N - Q - 1 will give the number of branches to be removed)

It was pretty straight forward to implement.\\

 1# include <cstdio>
 2# include <map>
 3# include <set>
 4# include <bitset>
 5using namespace std;
 6int N, Q;
 7unsigned long long Total = 0;
 8struct Branch
 9{
10 bool operator< (const Branch & branch) const
11 {
12  if (this->Apples == branch.Apples)
13  {
14   if (this->Start == branch.Start)
15    return this->End < branch.End;
16   return this->Start< branch.Start;
17  }
18  return this->Apples < branch.Apples;
19 }
20 Branch (int a, int b, int c){Start = a; End = b; Apples = c;}
21 int Start, End, Apples;
22};
23set <Branch> Edges;
24bitset <101> Visited;
25map <int, map <int, int> > Tree;
26void FindEdges (int current, int parent)
27{
28 //printf ("%d\t%d\n", current, parent);
29 if (Visited[current]) return;
30 //printf ("%d\t%d Not Visited\n", current, parent);
31 Visited[current] = true;
32 map<int, int>::iterator it = Tree[current].begin();
33 if (Tree[current].size() == 1)
34  Edges.insert (Branch (parent, current, Tree[parent][current]));
35 else
36  for (; it != Tree[current].end(); it++)
37   if (!Visited[it->first])
38    FindEdges (it->first, current);
39}
40int main()
41{
42 //freopen ("Input.txt", "r", stdin);
43 //freopen ("Scratch.txt", "w", stdout);
44 scanf ("%d%d", &N, &Q);
45 Q = N - 1 - Q;
46 int A, B, C;
47 for (int i = 0; i < N - 1; i++)
48 {
49  scanf ("%d%d%d", &A, &B, &C);
50  Tree[A][B] = C;
51  Tree[B][A] = C;
52  Total += C;
53 }
54 for (int i = 0; i < Q; i++)
55 {
56  Edges.clear();
57  Visited.reset();
58  map<int, int>::iterator it1 = Tree[1].begin();
59  Visited[1] = true;
60  for (; it1 != Tree[1].end(); it1++)
61   FindEdges(it1->first, 1);
62  //printf ("Edges Size : %lu\n", Edges.size());
63  set<Branch>::iterator it = Edges.begin();
64  //printf ("%d\t%d\t%d\n", it->Start, it->End, it->Apples);
65  Total -= it->Apples;
66  Tree[it->Start].erase (it->End);
67  Tree[it->End].erase (it->Start);
68 }
69 printf ("%llu\n", Total);
70}

However, this solution was failing so many times. Then I found the testcase for which this program was failing.

14 1
21 2 1
31 3 2
42 4 3

The above shown solution returns 1 as the result whereas the optimal result is 2. This approach is greedy approach I believe.
In the first iteration, it detects the branches

11 3 2
22 4 3

and removes the branch 1 3 2, since it has the least number of apples and in the next iteration it detects the following branch

12 4 3

since that is the only leaf branch available and it removes that, leaving us with the suboptimal solution 1.
\\ Here is the DP solution which can really solve this problem and this got accepted by Timus.
\\

 1#include <cstdio>
 2#include <cstring>
 3#include <vector>
 4#include <algorithm>
 5
 6using namespace std;
 7
 8int N,Q, Tree[101][101], DP[101][101];
 9int solve (int current, int parent, int q)
10{
11 if (q <= 0) return 0;
12 int lindex = -1, rindex = -1;
13 int & result = DP[current][q];
14 if (result != -1) return result;
15 for (int i = 0; i < 101; i++)
16  if (Tree[current][i] != -1 && i != parent) {lindex = i; break;}
17 for (int i = (lindex == -1?0:lindex+1); i < 101; i++)
18  if (Tree[current][i] != -1 && i != parent) {rindex = i; break;}
19 //printf ("%d\t%d\t%d\t%d\t%d\n", current, parent, lindex, rindex, q);
20 if (lindex == -1 || rindex == -1) return 0;
21 for (int i = 0; i <= q; i++)
22  result = max (result, (i == q?0:Tree[current][lindex] + solve(lindex, current, q - i - 1))
23   + (i == 0?0:Tree[current][rindex] + solve(rindex, current, i - 1)));
24 //printf ("Returning %d\n", result);
25 return result;
26}
27int main()
28{
29 //freopen ("Input.txt", "r", stdin);
30 //freopen ("Scratch.txt", "w", stdout);
31 scanf("%d%d",&N,&Q);
32 memset (Tree, -1, sizeof Tree);
33 memset (DP, -1, sizeof DP);
34 for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
35  for (int j = 0, x, y, z; j < N; j++)
36  {
37   scanf ("%d%d%d", &x, &y, &z);
38   Tree [x][y] = z;
39   Tree [y][x] = z;
40  }
41 printf ("%d\n", solve (1, 0, Q));
42 return 0;
43}

Please write to me if you want me to explain this program. We can do that over chat.

item.title: UVa 11259 - Coin Changing Again
item.description:
This took lot of my time and I managed to come up with this Top-down Dynamic Programming solution. This approach times out. Any suggestions? Problem Statement : http://uva.onlinejudge.org/index.php?option=com_onlinejudge&Itemid=8&page=show_problem&problem=2226\\

 1# include <cstdio>
 2# include <map>
 3# include <set>
 4using namespace std;
 5struct State
 6{
 7 State (int v1, int v2, int v3, int v4)
 8 {
 9  V1 = v1; V2 = v2; V3 = v3; V4 = v4;
10 }
11 int getPart2(int Value = 0)
12 {
13  int Part2 = 0;
14  Part2 = (V4 >> 13);
15  Part2 |= (Value << 4);
16  return Part2;
17 }
18 unsigned long long getPart1()
19 {
20  unsigned long long Part1 = 0;
21  Part1 = V1;
22  Part1 |= (V2 << 17);
23  Part1 |= ((unsigned long long)V3 << 34);
24  Part1 |= ((unsigned long long)V4 << 51);
25  return Part1;
26 }
27 int V1, V2, V3, V4;
28};
29map <int, set<unsigned long long> > States;
30map <int, set<unsigned long long> > Solutions;
31int c1, c2, c3, c4, q, d1, d2, d3, d4, v;
32unsigned long long Result ;
33bool CheckVisited (unsigned long long Part1, int Part2)
34{
35 if (States[Part2].count (Part1)) return true;
36 States[Part2].insert (Part1);
37 return false;
38}
39void Solution (State & s, int Value)
40{
41 unsigned long long Part1 = s.getPart1();
42 int Part2 = s.getPart2(Value);
43 if (!Value)
44 {
45  Solutions[Part2].insert (Part1);
46  return;
47 }
48 if (CheckVisited(Part1, Part2)) return;
49 if (s.V1 - 1 >= 0 && Value - c1 >= 0)
50 {
51  s.V1--;
52  Solution (s, Value - c1);
53  s.V1++;
54 }
55 if (s.V2 - 1 >= 0 && Value - c2 >= 0)
56 {
57  s.V2--;
58  Solution (s, Value - c2);
59  s.V2++;
60 }
61 if (s.V3 - 1 >= 0 && Value - c3 >= 0)
62 {
63  s.V3--;
64  Solution (s, Value - c3);
65  s.V3++;
66 }
67 if (s.V4 - 1 >= 0 && Value - c4 >= 0)
68 {
69  s.V4--;
70  Solution (s, Value - c4);
71  s.V4++;
72 }
73}
74int main()
75{
76 freopen ("Input.txt", "r", stdin);
77 freopen ("Scratch.txt", "w", stdout);
78 int N;
79 scanf ("%d", &N);
80 State s (0, 0, 0, 0);
81 while (N--)
82 {
83  scanf ("%d%d%d%d%d", &c1, &c2, &c3, &c4, &q);
84  while (q--)
85  {
86   scanf ("%d%d%d%d%d", &s.V1, &s.V2, &s.V3, &s.V4, &v);
87   Result = 0;
88   States.clear();
89   Solutions.clear();
90   Solution (s, v);
91   for (map<int, set<unsigned long long> >::iterator it = Solutions.begin(); it != Solutions.end(); it++)
92    Result += it->second.size();
93   printf ("%lld\n", Result);
94  }
95 }
96}

item.title: Number of ways to change making (Dynamic Programming)
item.description:
This is a variant of change making problem. Here, we are just asked to count the number of ways to make the specific change. With a little change to the change making problem's solution, we can solve this one. The problems which can be solved with the following solution are

UVa - 657 - Coin Change

UVa - 357 - Let Me Count The Ways (Need to change the way solution is printed as per problem description)

 1# include <iostream>
 2# include <cstdio>
 3using namespace std;
 4unsigned long long NumberOfWays [30001], Coins []= {1, 5, 10, 25, 50}, Num;
 5int main ()
 6{
 7 //freopen ("Input.txt", "r", stdin);
 8 //freopen ("Scratch.txt", "w", stdout);
 9 NumberOfWays[0] = 1;
10 for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
11  for (int j = Coins[i]; j < 30001; j++)
12   NumberOfWays [j] += NumberOfWays [j - Coins[i]];
13 while (scanf ("%lld", &Num) != EOF)
14  printf ("%lld\n", NumberOfWays[Num]); //Change this for UVa - 357 - Let Me Count The Ways
15}

item.title: Change Making (Dynamic Programming) Problem
item.description:
This is a classic change making problem.
A variant of the same problem, counting the number of ways to make the change is here

Problem Name : Making Change
Problem ID   : 2768
Problem URL  : http://acm.tju.edu.cn/toj/showp2768.html
Solution     :

 1# include <iostream>
 2# include <cstdio>
 3# include <cstring>
 4# include <algorithm>
 5int denoms [10];
 6int change [1001];
 7using namespace std;
 8int main()
 9{
10 //freopen ("Input.txt", "r", stdin);
11 //freopen ("Scratch.txt", "w", stdout);
12 int C, N;
13 scanf ("%d%d", &C, &N);
14 fill (change, change + C + 1, 10000);
15 for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) scanf ("%d", &denoms[i]);
16 sort (denoms, denoms + N);
17 change[0] = 0;
18 for (int j = 0; j < N; j++)
19  for (int i = denoms[j]; i <= C; i++)
20   change[i] = min (change[i], change[i - denoms[j]] + 1);
21 printf ("%d\n", change[C]);
22}
